flashcard_questions.a: The minimum stock level, the lowest safe amount a business holds.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the re-order level on a stock graph?
flashcard_questions.a: The point at which new stock must be ordered.
The gap between placing an order and the stock arriving.
Partly finished goods still moving through production.

flashcard_questions.q: What is just in time stock control?
flashcard_questions.a: Parts and materials arrive at the factory exactly as they are needed.
The process of buying in what a business needs to operate.
Organising the transport of raw materials and finished goods to where they are needed.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the lead time when a shop re-orders at week 1.5 and stock arrives at week 2?
What is the pet shop's buffer stock level for cat food?
What cash-flow advantage does just in time give a business?
flashcard_questions.a: Money is not tied up in unsold stock.

flashcard_questions.q: What happens to a just in time production line if one delivery is late?
flashcard_questions.a: Production stops, because there is no buffer stock.

flashcard_questions.q: Which discount does a business lose by ordering in small just in time quantities?
Why is holding too much stock expensive for a business?
flashcard_questions.a: It must rent and run warehouse space.

flashcard_questions.q: What happened to KFC in 2018 after it switched logistics provider?
flashcard_questions.a: Chicken shortages closed hundreds of UK restaurants temporarily.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is the lowest-priced supplier not always the best value?
flashcard_questions.a: A dearer supplier that delivers reliably can save money long term.
